title: Grace and works
hook: Catholics and Lutherans agreed in 1999 that we're saved by grace, not by works, and good works follow

segments.voice: Yesterday, repentance: metanoia, pulling over and turning the car around. Your line was turn and be forgiven. What small thing did you turn? Day three hundred nine.

Augsburg, Germany. October 31, 1999. Four hundred eighty-two years to the day after Martin Luther sent off his ninety-five theses. In a church in the city where Lutherans had first presented their confession of faith to the emperor, in 1530, leaders of the Lutheran World Federation and of the Catholic Church sit down at a table and sign a document together. For almost five centuries, the two churches had formally condemned each other's teaching on how a person is made right with God. Wars had been fought partly over it. Families split. Now, they sign a statement saying: on the heart of this question, we agree. Not on everything. But on the center. Today's word is what they agreed on.
screen: `AUGSBURG, OCTOBER 31, 1999.` → `482 YEARS TO THE DAY.` → `ON THE CENTER, WE AGREE.`

segments.voice: Justification is a courtroom word. To justify someone is to declare them in the right. In the Bible, the question is: how does a person come to be right with God? Paul's answer, in Ephesians, is the line we read on day two hundred eighty-nine: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." And the very next lines go on: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." Grace first. Then good. But James, in his letter, says bluntly: "faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." For centuries, Protestants and Catholics heard those texts pulling in different directions. Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous, as a free gift received by faith alone. Catholics stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous from within, and that grace works through a changed life. Each suspected the other of missing something. The Joint Declaration of 1999 said, in its own careful words: by grace alone, in faith in what Christ has done, and not because of anything we deserve, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works. Both sides agreed that the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as the other now presents it. They still differ in how they describe some things, and some theologians on both sides objected. But since then, Methodists, Anglicans and Reformed churches have added their names too. The order everyone now agreed on is simple enough to fit in a pocket. Grace comes first. Good works grow out of it, the way fruit grows on a tree that is already alive.
screen: `JUSTIFY: DECLARE IN THE RIGHT.` · `EPHESIANS 2, AND JAMES 2.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · `1999: ON THE CENTER, AGREED.` · then, large: `CREATED IN CHRIST JESUS UNTO GOOD WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a good work out of gratitude. Settle, and breathe. First, remember something you've been given that you didn't earn. Stay with it until you actually feel thankful. Then, out of that thankfulness, not out of guilt or to prove anything, choose one good thing to do today. Something small and specific: a call, a meal, a note, a chore done for someone else. If you pray, you can thank God for grace, and offer the good work as thanks. If you don't, just let gratitude choose it. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Being made right with God. Catholics and Lutherans now agree: by grace, through faith, and good works follow.
Your line: grace first, then good. Today, do your good work, and notice that it feels different when it comes from thanks instead of fear. Day three hundred nine.

screen: `DAY 309 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY.`

howItsDone: Christians of many churches describe good works, such as serving the poor, giving and caring for neighbors, as a grateful response to God's grace, and some churches mark Reformation Day on October 31 with joint Catholic–Lutheran prayer.

original.note: Greek: to justify, to declare or make righteous. Paul's word in Romans and Galatians.
